Slides (black), the doctor's notes (green), every gift (red) and the Aldughaither summary of the large intestine (grey, at the end).

Epidemiology & aetiology

  • The most common cancer affecting males in Saudi Arabia. Lifetime risk ~5%; males slightly higher; rectum and sigmoid are particularly common sites.
  • One affected first-degree relative → ~2× risk. Most CRCs are adenocarcinomas. Risk: family history, chronic inflammation (IBD), high fat/meat/calorie intake, obesity, age (rises after 40–45), hereditary syndromes. Mechanism: prolonged mucosal contact with luminal toxins — hence the protective effect of fibre and physical activity.
  • Proven risk factor for colon cancer → ulcerative colitis. 429 ×3
  • IMA supplies → distal ⅓ transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, upper rectum. 441

Adenoma–carcinoma sequence & polyps

  • Benign polyp → cancer takes 7–10 years; risk depends on type of polyp, size, and multiple polyps (greater risk).
  • Polyp = a mass projecting into the lumen. Macroscopic: pedunculated, sessile, flat. Microscopic: tubular, tubulovillous, villous.
  • Adenomas affect 40% of people > 50 and 70% of those 65–69. Tubular 75% (often pedunculated), villous 10%, tubulovillous 15%.
  • The years-long interval is the basis of screening. A single small polyp's malignant risk is < 2%, but we can't tell which — all adenomas are removed.
PolypMalignant potential (doctor)
HyperplasticLittle/none — not premalignant
Tubular adenomaLowest of the adenomas (most common)
TubulovillousIntermediate
Villous adenomaHighest
  • Premalignant colorectal polyp → adenomatous. 429 ×3

Polypectomy & the malignant polyp

  • Colonoscopic polypectomy is the treatment of choice. Invasion into the submucosa = malignant polyp.
  • Polypectomy is enough if: free margin ≥ 2 mm, well/moderately differentiated, no lymphovascular invasion, no tumour budding — otherwise segmental resection.
  • Tumour budding = clusters of malignant cells in the submucosa remote from the main invasive front.
  • Notes: malignant polyp with margin < 1 mm → formal oncological resection. Tumour budding is an adverse feature.
  • Malignant sessile polyp (adenocarcinoma) after endoscopic removal → keyed segmental resection. 438
Invasion starts at the submucosa (T1) — the first layer with lymphatics, so that's where nodal spread becomes possible.

Presentation

  • Non-specific symptoms.
Right colonLeft colonRectum
LumenLarge — grows big before obstructingSmaller — obstructs earlierReservoir disturbed
Classic pictureIron-deficiency anaemia, fatigue, pain, occult bloodChange in bowel habit, obstructionFresh bleeding, tenesmus
Iron-deficiency anaemia in an adult (male or post-menopausal woman) = right-sided colon cancer until proven otherwise.
  • Tired, breathless, Hb 8.5, mobile mass → carcinoma of the caecum. 437 ×2
  • Rectal bleeding, weight loss, mass at 10 cm on DRE → rectal cancer 442 ×2; bright red blood mixed with stool, weight loss, constipation → colon cancer. 436 ×6
  • Mass involving the appendix and caecum, biopsy adenocarcinoma → right hemicolectomy. 442
  • 20-year-old with haemorrhoids, family history of colon cancer and iron-deficiency anaemia → colonoscopy. 439 ×17

Screening

  • Screening colonoscopy from age 45 (latest recommendation). Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice (biopsy + removal).
  • Faecal occult blood with sigmoidoscopy is another option. CT colonography lacks biopsy/snaring. Barium enema — not any more.
  • Average risk: start ~45; normal → repeat every 10 years; family/personal history or polyps → ~5 years. FIT preferred over old FOBT (positive → colonoscopy; negative → annually). Faecal calprotectin is NOT a CRC test (IBD vs IBS). Screening a 20-year-old isn't justified unless there is a hereditary syndrome.
  • Average-risk screening → colonoscopy every 10 years from 45–50. 441

Hereditary CRC

  • Most CRC is sporadic; ~10% genetic. HNPCC (Lynch) — 3–5% of inherited disorders; right-sided, young.
  • ~95% sporadic, ~5% familial (Lynch, FAP). Finding the gene lets relatives be screened early.
  • Lynch (Amsterdam) criteria → 3 relatives, 2 successive generations, 1 a first-degree relative, 1 diagnosed < 50 (and FAP excluded). 441
  • FAP — start sigmoidoscopy screening at 10–12 years. 441 ×2
  • 28-year-old with hundreds of polyps → proctocolectomy with ileoanal pouch (colectomy + IRA is an option if the rectum is spared). 434 ×2
  • Long-standing UC with sigmoid adenocarcinoma → proctocolectomy 441; UC 10 years with high-grade dysplasia in a polyp → total proctocolectomy with ileoanal J-pouch. 438 ×8

Work-up & staging

  • After biopsy: staging work-up — CBC, U&E, LFT, coagulation, CEA, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; rectal cancer → MRI pelvis ± EUS. PET-CT can find unsuspected metastases. Tumour board (MDT).
  • Always stage first. CEA is NOT diagnostic (raised in smokers, benign disease; normal doesn't exclude CRC; normal ~0–5). Uses: prognosis, response to treatment, and detecting recurrence (rising CEA → CT).
  • PET isn't for screening or routine staging — for known metastatic disease (if it changes management) or rising CEA with a negative CT.
  • Staging of a splenic-flexure adenocarcinoma → CT chest, abdomen and pelvis 429 ×3; CEA is most useful for → surveillance for recurrence 437 ×3 441 ×2
  • Tumour marker for a rectal carcinoid → chromogranin A. 439

Pathology & TNM

  • Differentiation: well, moderately, poorly; lymph node involvement.
TInvasion
TisMucosa only
T1Submucosa
T2Muscularis propria
T3Full thickness / perirectal (pericolic) fat
T4Adjacent organs
  • Minimum 12 lymph nodes. N1 = 1–3 nodes; N2 = ≥ 4 nodes; M1 = distant organ (liver, peritoneum, lung).
  • ≥ 12 negative nodes → < 1% chance of a missed positive node. < 12 = understaging → high-risk feature.

Treatment

  • Surgery is the most important variable; radiation and chemotherapy alone cannot cure any stage. The site of the tumour dictates the procedure.
  • Pre-op: NPO, IVF, mechanical bowel prep, chemical prep (oral/IV antibiotics), cross-match, DVT prophylaxis, ICU booking, stoma marking, consent.
  • In the OR: sign in, epidural, Foley, position, pneumatic devices, prep & drape, time out.
  • Principles: examine the entire abdomen · remove the segment with adequate margins · remove the corresponding lymph nodes · open vs laparoscopic.
  • Margins ~5 cm proximal and distal; mesentery along the feeding vessels; ≥ 12 nodes. Stoma site marked before surgery — visible to the patient, on a flat surface, away from creases and bony prominences.

Resections: right hemicolectomy, left hemicolectomy, abdominoperineal resection, anterior resection, low anterior resection, subtotal colectomy

  • Complications: bleeding, infection, collection, leak, adjacent visceral injury — ureter, gonadal vessels, spleen (left-sided); duodenum (right-sided).
  • Synchronous sigmoid and rectal cancers → anterior resection (both in one specimen). 441

Who gets additional treatment?

  • Colon: all stage III (positive nodes) → adjuvant chemotherapy; high-risk stage II (T3/T4) — clinical: obstruction, perforation; pathological: poorly differentiated, mucinous, LV invasion, Nx.
  • Rectum (up to 15 cm from the anal verge): all T3–4 and any node involvement → neoadjuvant radiation → surgery → chemo (non-metastatic).
StageDefinitionChemotherapy
IT1–T2 N0Surgery alone
IIT3–T4 N0Only if high-risk features
IIIAny N+Adjuvant chemo
IVDistant metastasisSystemic therapy central
High-risk stage II features: < 12 nodes · poor differentiation · lymphovascular invasion · perineural invasion · T4 · obstruction · perforation.
  • T3N0 after sigmoidectomy with only 6 nodes examined → chemotherapy (inadequate nodes = high risk). 438
  • Chemotherapy given after resection → adjuvant. 435
  • Rectal cancer gets radiotherapy; colon cancer doesn't — the rectum's high local recurrence risk. T1 N0 → local excision (no RT); ≥ T2 or N+ → radiotherapy. Selected complete responders → watch-and-wait.
  • Rectal cancer at 10 cm, T3N1M0 → keyed radiotherapy (neoadjuvant chemoradiation, then surgery). 438 ×6
  • Role of neoadjuvant radiation in T3N1 rectal cancer → keyed to down-stage the tumour 436; role of neoadjuvant radiotherapy → local control. 435 ×2

Obstruction & metastatic disease

  • Metastasectomy depends on the organ affected.
  • Metastatic CRC is an MDT disease (colorectal, HPB, thoracic surgeons, oncologists). An obstructing primary may need treating first.
  • LBO in a 65-year-old with no previous surgery → malignancy. 433 ×2
  • Fit 65-year-old with an obstructing sigmoid tumour → Hartmann's operation. 429
  • Obstructing ultra-low rectal mass with liver, lung and nodal metastases → stoma 437 ×3; 89-year-old, obstructing sigmoid cancer with liver and lung metastases → keyed colectomy. 439

Follow-up

  • Office visit every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months for 3 years; regular CEA; colonoscopy at year 1, if normal after 3 years, then every 5 years; CT yearly for 5 years.
  • Recurrence risk is highest in the first 5 years, especially the first 2.

GIST, carcinoid & mucocele

  • GIST: submucosal; c-KIT mutation (transmembrane tyrosine-kinase receptor); from cells of Cajal; wide surgical resection; imatinib if necrosis, > 5 cm, mitoses > 5; high-risk sites (duodenum, low rectum) may need neoadjuvant treatment.
  • GIST spreads haematogenously, not nodally — routine lymphadenectomy isn't central.
  • Carcinoid: APUD, submucosal, produces 5-HT (serotonin); carcinoid syndrome if liver metastases (flushing, diarrhoea, heart, respiratory); 24-h urinary 5-HIAA and blood chromogranin A; CT arterial enhancement, octreotide scan; surgery is the main treatment, even debulking.
  • Carcinoid syndrome needs liver metastases because the liver clears bowel serotonin (first pass). Imaging: somatostatin-receptor PET (DOTATATE).
  • Mucocele: dilated appendix filled with mucin — appendectomy is enough; no need for right hemicolectomy (most are benign).
  • Rupture of a malignant mucinous neoplasm → pseudomyxoma peritonei — needs formal oncological resection.

Large Intestine

Anatomy of the Colon and Rectum
1. Overview
  • The colon begins at the ileocecal valve and ends at the rectum, measuring approximately 140 cm (5 feet) in length.
  • It has both intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal components.
  • Retroperitoneal: Cecum, ascending, and descending colon.
  • Intraperitoneal: Transverse and sigmoid colon.
  • The cecum has the largest lumen (~7 cm) but the thinnest wall, making it most prone to ischemic necrosis and perforation.
2. Layers of the Colon Wall
There are four main layers:
1. Mucosa (innermost)
  • Lined with simple columnar epithelium forming crypts.
  • Contains lamina propria and muscularis mucosa.

2. Submucosa (strength layer)

  • Rich in collagen and blood vessels.
  • Important to include in anastomosis for better healing.

3. Muscularis Propria (smooth muscle layer)

  • Inner circular layer.
  • Outer longitudinal layer: Thickened into three taeniae coli.

4. Serosa (outermost layer)

  • Contains epiploic appendages (fat-filled pouches).
3. Key Anatomical Features
A. Taeniae Coli
  • Three longitudinal muscle bands that help form haustra (sacculations of the colon).
  • The appendix is located where the taeniae coli converge.
B. Rectum
  • Length: 12-16 cm.
  • Transitions from colon to rectum at the rectosigmoid junction.
  • Differences from colon:
  • No taenia coli (longitudinal muscle forms a continuous layer).
  • No haustra or epiploic appendages.
  • Location:
  • Upper rectum → Intraperitoneal.
  • Mid and lower rectum → Extraperitoneal.
  • Peritoneal reflections:
  • Pouch of Douglas (rectovesical in men, rectouterine in women) → Palpable on rectal or vaginal exam.
  • Denonvilliers’ fascia → Separates rectum from prostate & seminal vesicles (men) or cervix (women).
C. Pelvic Floor Muscles (Levator Ani)
  • Pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, puborectalis.
  • Puborectalis forms a sling at the anorectal junction, aiding in continence.
4. Blood Supply & Lymphatic Drainage
A. Arterial Supply
  • Embryological origin dictates vascular supply:
  • Midgut-derived (proximal colon) → Superior mesenteric artery (SMA).
  • Hindgut-derived (distal colon & rectum) → Inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).
ArterySupplies
Superior Mesenteric ArteryCecum, ascending, & transverse colon
(SMA)
Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA)Descending, sigmoid colon, upper rectum
Internal Iliac ArteryMiddle & lower rectum (via rectal arteries)
Marginal Artery of DrummondContinuous collateral circulation along colon
Arc of RiolanConnects SMA & IMA (redundancy in blood
supply)
  • Weak points:
  • "Watershed areas" (prone to ischemia): 1. Splenic flexure (Griffith’s point) → Between SMA & IMA. 2. Rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck’s point) → Between IMA & rectal arteries.
B. Venous Drainage
  • Follows arterial supply.
  • Inferior mesenteric vein (IMV) joins splenic vein, which drains into the portal system.
C. Lymphatic Drainage
  • Follows blood supply.
  • Oncologic resections follow vascular territories due to lymphatic spread of cancer.
5. Nerve Supply
  • Divided into two systems: 1. Midgut (proximal to transverse colon)
    • Sympathetic → T6-T12 (via SMA plexus).
    • Parasympathetic → Vagus nerve.
  • 2. Hindgut (distal transverse colon to rectum)
    • Sympathetic → L1-L3 (via IMA plexus).
    • Parasympathetic → Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4).
  • Key nerve structures:
  • Auerbach’s (myenteric) plexus → Controls motility.
  • Meissner’s (submucosal) plexus → Regulates secretions, blood flow, and absorption.
  • Surgical relevance:
  • Hypogastric nerves (L1-L3) → At risk during IMA ligation.
  • Inferior hypogastric plexus → At risk in rectal surgery → Injury can cause bladder & sexual dysfunction.
6. Clinical & Surgical Relevance
A. Importance of Blood Supply
  • Watershed areas prone to ischemia:
  • Splenic flexure infarction (ischemic colitis).
  • Rectosigmoid infarction in low-flow states (e.g., shock, heart failure).
B. Weak Points in Colon Wall
  • Cecum → Thinnest wall, highest risk of perforation (esp. in large bowel obstruction).
  • Diverticula form at weak points where vasa recta penetrate the muscularis propria.
C. Surgical Considerations
  • Oncologic colon resection:
  • Must include lymphatics & vascular territories.
  • “High ligation” of vessels ensures complete cancer resection.
  • Rectal surgery risks:
  • Pelvic nerve injury → Leads to bladder & sexual dysfunction.
  • Denonvilliers’ fascia dissection must be carefully performed.
Large Bowel Obstruction (LBO)
1. General Considerations
  • Accounts for ~15% of intestinal obstructions in adults.
  • Incidence increases with age.
  • Causes:
  • Intrinsic bowel wall pathology: Colorectal cancer (most common), strictures (diverticulitis, IBD, ischemia, radiation, surgical anastomosis).
  • Mechanical causes: Volvulus, incarcerated hernia, intussusception.
  • Intraluminal obstruction: Fecal impaction, foreign bodies.
  • Colonic adhesions are a rare cause, unlike in small bowel obstruction.
  • Differential diagnosis:
  • Pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome): Functional colonic dilation without mechanical obstruction.
Role of the Ileocecal Valve
  • Competent ileocecal valve (70% of cases) → Closed-loop obstruction.
  • Prevents decompression into the ileum → Rapid intraluminal pressure rise.
  • High risk of cecal ischemia, necrosis, perforation.
  • Incompetent ileocecal valve (30% of cases) → Allows decompression into the small intestine.
  • Symptoms may mimic small bowel obstruction.
2. Clinical Findings
A. Symptoms & Signs
  • Obstipation (absolute constipation):
  • Universal in complete obstruction.
  • May still pass stool distal to the obstruction initially.
  • Abdominal pain:
  • Crampy, deep visceral pain in the hypogastrium.
  • Slow-growing right-sided lesions may be painless until late-stage obstruction.
  • Acute obstruction (volvulus, hernia, intussusception) → Sudden, severe pain.
  • Abdominal distention:
  • More severe than small bowel obstruction.
  • Vomiting (late finding):
  • May not occur if the ileocecal valve remains competent.
  • If vomiting is present, suggests severe obstruction with small bowel involvement.
  • Rectal exam:
  • Empty vault except in distal fecal impaction.
  • Systemic signs of ischemia/perforation:
  • Fever, leukocytosis, peritonitis → Suggests gangrene or perforation.
  • Sepsis and acidosis → Indicates bacterial translocation.
3. Imaging Studies
A. Abdominal X-ray (First-line)
  • Dilated colon:
  • Haustral markings distinguish colon from small intestine.
  • Key findings:
  • Sigmoid volvulus → "Coffee bean sign".
  • Cecal volvulus → Dilated loop in the RLQ extending medially.
  • No gas distal to obstruction → Complete obstruction.
B. CT scan with Rectal Contrast (Gold Standard)
  • Identifies:
  • Transition point.
  • Cause of obstruction (tumor, volvulus, stricture, hernia, etc.).
  • Complications (ischemia, perforation).
  • Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) is used if strangulation/perforation is suspected.
4. Treatment
A. Goals of Management

1. Decompress the obstructed bowel.

2. Resect any necrotic bowel.

3. Remove the underlying cause (if possible in one operation).

4. Restore bowel continuity (if feasible). 5. Consider stenting for palliation or as a bridge to surgery.

B. Surgical Management 1. Right-Sided Obstructions (Cecum, Ascending Colon)

  • Most cases can be managed in one stage with:
  • Right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis (if the patient is stable).
  • If unstable or perforated:
    • Resection with ileostomy and mucous fistula.
    • Delayed anastomosis in a second stage.
2. Left-Sided Obstructions (Descending, Sigmoid Colon)
  • More commonly require diversion.
  • Approaches:
  • Hartmann’s procedure (Resection with end colostomy & rectal stump).
  • Resection with primary anastomosis (if stable).
  • Loop colostomy or ileostomy (if resection is not feasible).
C. Stent Placement
  • Indications:
  • Palliative → Unresectable colorectal cancer.
  • Bridge to surgery → Allows for decompression before definitive resection.
  • Risks:
  • Perforation (rare but serious).
  • Re-obstruction over time.
5. Prognosis
  • Depends on:
  • Patient’s age & comorbidities.
  • Extent of ischemia/necrosis.
  • Presence of perforation/sepsis.
  • Cause of obstruction.
  • Timeliness of surgical intervention.
Key Prognostic Factors
  • Cecal diameter > 12 cm → High risk of perforation.
  • Delays in surgery (>24 hours post-diagnosis) → Higher mortality.
  • Malignant obstruction → Worse outcomes if metastatic.
Acute Colonic Pseudo-Obstruction (Ogilvie Syndrome)
1. General Considerations
  • Characterized by massive colonic dilation in the absence of a mechanical obstruction.
  • Most commonly affects hospitalized, critically ill patients.
  • Often occurs in:
  • Postoperative patients.
  • Severe medical conditions: Cardiac disease, trauma, sepsis, electrolyte disturbances.
  • Medication-related causes: Narcotics, anticholinergics.
Pathophysiology
  • Severe form of ileus affecting the colon.
  • Autonomic dysfunction → Loss of colonic motility.
  • Predominantly affects the right and transverse colon.
2. Clinical Findings
A. Symptoms & Signs
  • Gradual, progressive abdominal distension (over days).
  • Later symptoms:
  • Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting.
  • Obstipation (may still pass stool/gas if partial).
  • Diarrhea in 40% of cases (unlike mechanical obstruction).
  • Systemic symptoms (if ischemia/perforation occurs):
  • Fever, leukocytosis, worsening pain, peritonitis.
B. Differential Diagnosis
  • Toxic Megacolon (IBD, C. difficile colitis).
  • Mechanical Large Bowel Obstruction (colorectal cancer, volvulus, hernia).
  • Paralytic Ileus (generalized GI hypomotility post-surgery).
C. Imaging
  • Abdominal X-ray (First-line):
  • Massive colonic dilation, often in the right and transverse colon.
  • CT scan with Rectal Contrast (Gold Standard):
  • Differentiates true obstruction from pseudo-obstruction.
  • Rules out ischemia, perforation.
  • Excludes volvulus, malignancy.
  • Water-soluble contrast enema (Alternative if CT unavailable).
  • Stops when the dilated colon is reached to prevent perforation.
3. Treatment
A. Initial Conservative Management (First 48 Hours)
  • Fluid resuscitation.
  • Correct electrolyte imbalances (K+, Mg2+, Ca2+).
  • Stop offending medications (narcotics, anticholinergics).
  • Treat underlying conditions (sepsis, cardiac disease, respiratory failure).
  • Serial abdominal exams & imaging to monitor for ischemia/perforation.
  • Success rate: 70%-90% with conservative measures.

B. Pharmacologic Management (If No Improvement in 48 Hours) Neostigmine (First-line Drug Therapy)

  • Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor → Increases colonic motility.
  • Indication: No response to conservative management within 48 hours.
  • Administration:
  • IV infusion over 5 minutes.
  • Requires continuous cardiac monitoring (risk of bradycardia).
  • Rectal tube should be placed before administration.
  • Success rate: ~90%.
  • Contraindications:
  • Bradycardia.
  • Bronchospasm (asthma, COPD).
  • Severe renal impairment.
  • Pregnancy.
  • Side Effects: Abdominal cramps, excessive salivation, vomiting.

If no response, a second dose can be given after 30–60 minutes.

C. Endoscopic Decompression (If Neostigmine Fails)
  • Allows direct visualization of the mucosa (checks for ischemia).
  • Success rate: ~80%.
  • Risk of perforation: ~2% (higher in inexperienced centers).
  • Recurrence rate: 10%-30%.
  • Alternative to neostigmine in patients with contraindications.
D. Surgical Intervention (For Refractory Cases)
Indications for Surgery:
  • Colonic ischemia or perforation.
  • Cecal diameter >12 cm for >6 days → High risk of perforation.
  • Failure of neostigmine & endoscopic decompression.
Surgical Options:

1. Percutaneous cecostomy (for decompression in high-risk patients).

2. Loop transverse colostomy (if cecostomy is not feasible).

3. Resection with end colostomy (if ischemia/perforation occurs).

4. Primary anastomosis (rare, only in select cases without sepsis).

4. Prognosis
  • Overall mortality: ~8%.
  • If ischemia or perforation occurs → Mortality rises to ~40%.
  • Early diagnosis & treatment significantly improve outcomes.
Colon Cancer and Polyps
1. Background
  • Third most common cancer in the U.S. (after prostate and lung cancer in men, breast and lung cancer in women).
  • 140,000 new cases & 50,000 deaths annually (as of 2018).
  • Risk Factors:
  • Non-Modifiable: Family history, personal history of adenomatous polyps or IBD (especially pancolitis), diabetes, truncal obesity.
  • Modifiable: High red/processed meat diet, smoking, alcohol.
  • Genetics:
  • Three major pathways for CRC development:

1. Chromosomal instability (75%) → Classic "adenoma-to-carcinoma"

  • sequence.

2. Microsatellite instability (15%) → Lynch syndrome & sporadic cases.

3. CpG island methylator phenotype (20%) → Right-sided, serrated polyp

  • pathway.
2. Hereditary Colorectal Cancer Syndromes
A. Lynch Syndrome (Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer, HNPCC)
  • Most common hereditary CRC syndrome (autosomal dominant).
  • Increased risk of extracolonic cancers:
  • Endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urinary tract, biliary, small bowel, pancreatic, breast, prostate, and CNS (glioblastoma).
  • Gene Mutations:
  • Mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) → Causes microsatellite instability.
  • Lifetime CRC risk: 10%-74% (MSH2 & MLH1 mutations have the highest risk).
  • Average CRC diagnosis age: 44-61 years.
  • Screening Guidelines:
  • Colonoscopy every 1-2 years starting at age 20-25.
  • Endometrial & ovarian cancer screening +/- prophylactic hysterectomy/oophorectomy.
  • Consider gastric, pancreatic, and urinary tract screening.
  • Surgical Management:
  • Total abdominal colectomy or total proctocolectomy in high-risk cases.
  • Segmental colectomy carries high risk of metachronous cancer (40% at 20 years).
B. Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)
  • Autosomal dominant disorder caused by APC mutation (chromosome 5q21).
  • 100-1000+ adenomatous polyps develop by age 15.
  • Lifetime CRC risk: 100% by age 39.
  • Variant: Attenuated FAP (aFAP) → Fewer polyps (<100), 70% CRC risk, later onset (~58 years).
  • Screening Guidelines:
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy at age 12 (colonoscopy if polyps present).
  • Annual endoscopic surveillance of rectum or ileal pouch after colectomy.
  • Surgical Management:
  • Prophylactic colectomy is recommended:
    • Total proctocolectomy with end ileostomy (for extensive disease).
    • Restorative proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA).
    • Total abdominal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis (if rectal polyp burden is low).
  • Extracolonic Manifestations:
  • Duodenal cancer risk (4-12%) → Upper endoscopy at 20-25 years.
  • Desmoid tumors (5%) → Major cause of death in FAP.
  • Other risks: Medulloblastoma, thyroid cancer, hepatoblastoma, gastric polyps.
C. MUTYH-Associated Polyposis (MAP)
  • Autosomal recessive polyposis syndrome.
  • MUTYH gene mutation (base excision repair defect).
  • Typically <100 adenomas (similar to aFAP).
  • CRC risk: >70%, with median age of diagnosis ~45-55 years.
  • Extracolonic cancer risk: Bladder, ovarian, skin, thyroid cancers.
  • Screening & Management:
  • Colonoscopy every 1-2 years starting at age 25-30.
  • Upper endoscopy at age 30, repeated every 3-5 years.
  • Surgical treatment similar to FAP if CRC risk is high or polyps become unmanageable.
D. Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome (JPS)
  • Autosomal dominant disorder (SMAD4, BMPR1A mutations).
  • Characterized by non-adenomatous (hamartomatous) polyps.
  • Risk of CRC: 39%-68% (median age of onset 43 years).
  • Diagnosis:
  • ≥5 juvenile polyps or any number with a family history.
  • Associated Syndromes:
  • Cronkhite-Canada Syndrome (JPS + ectodermal abnormalities).
  • Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba Syndrome (JPS + macrocephaly + genital pigmentation).
  • Cowden Syndrome (JPS + thyroid/breast cancer).
  • Screening & Management:
  • Colonoscopy at 12-15 years, upper endoscopy at 15-25 years.
  • Surgery if high-grade dysplasia or failure of endoscopic polyp removal.
E. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS)
  • Autosomal dominant disorder (STK11 mutation, chromosome 19).
  • Characterized by:
  • Hamartomatous polyps (small bowel, stomach, colon, rectum).
  • Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation (perioral, hands, feet, genitals).
  • Lifetime CRC risk: 39%.
  • High risk for:
  • Breast, pancreatic, ovarian, gastric, cervical, testicular cancers.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Perioral pigmentation + family history OR ≥2 PJS polyps.
  • Screening:
  • Small bowel imaging & testicular exams at 8-10 years.
  • Colonoscopy, upper endoscopy, cervical cancer screening in late teens.
  • Pancreatic cancer screening at 30-35 years.
  • Management:
  • Endoscopic removal if possible, otherwise surgical resection.
3. Colorectal Cancer Diagnosis & Management
A. Symptoms
  • Right-sided tumors: Iron deficiency anemia, occult bleeding, vague pain.
  • Left-sided tumors: Change in bowel habits, obstructive symptoms.
  • Rectal tumors: Tenesmus, hematochezia, sensation of incomplete evacuation.
B. Diagnosis
  • Colonoscopy with biopsy (Gold standard).
  • CT Colonography (if colonoscopy not possible).
  • Staging: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, CEA marker.
C. Treatment
  • Surgery (curative for localized disease):
  • Right hemicolectomy (cecum, ascending colon, proximal transverse colon).
  • Left hemicolectomy (distal transverse, descending colon).
  • Sigmoid colectomy (sigmoid cancer).
  • Low anterior resection (rectosigmoid, upper rectal tumors).
  • Abdominoperineal resection (lower rectal tumors with sphincter involvement).
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy (Stage III or high-risk Stage II).
  • Radiation (for rectal cancer).
Colorectal Cancer Screening Guidelines
1. Importance of Screening
  • Early detection reduces mortality
  • Prevention by removal of precancerous adenomas
  • 40-60% reduction in CRC mortality with screening
  • Higher benefit in high-risk individuals
2. Recommended Screening Tests

The U.S. Multi-Society Task Force (MSTF) 2017 Guidelines classify screening options into Tier 1 (preferred), Tier 2, and Tier 3 (alternative options).

A. Tier 1 (Preferred Tests)
1️- Colonoscopy (every 10 years)
  • Pros: Direct visualization, polyp removal, biopsy
  • Cons: Requires bowel prep, sedation, cost, risk of perforation (0.1%), bleeding (0.3%)
  • Best for: Prevention and early detection
2️- Fecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) (annually)
  • Pros: Non-invasive, no bowel prep, low cost (~$20)
  • Cons: Detects cancer (80% sensitivity), but misses many adenomas (~30% sensitivity)
  • Best for: Early detection (not prevention)
B. Tier 2 (Alternative Tests)
3️- CT Colonography (Virtual Colonoscopy) (every 5 years)
  • Pros: 80% sensitivity for large polyps (>1 cm), non-invasive
  • Cons: Requires full bowel prep, misses flat polyps, incidental extracolonic findings (5-15%), need for follow-up colonoscopy if polyps are found
4️- FIT-Fecal DNA Test (every 3 years)
  • Pros: Detects CRC with high sensitivity (>90%), some detection of advanced adenomas (~40%)
  • Cons: Lower specificity, high cost (~10× FIT cost), not widely used
5️- Flexible Sigmoidoscopy (every 5-10 years)
  • Pros: Good for left-sided cancers, lower risk than colonoscopy
  • Cons: Misses 30% of advanced adenomas, requires bowel prep, uncomfortable
  • Best for: Older patients, lower colon visualization only
C. Tier 3 (Limited Use)
6️- Capsule Colonoscopy
  • Not FDA-approved for routine screening
  • Used for: Patients with incomplete colonoscopies or contraindications to CT colonography

Treatment of Colon Cancer
1. Overview
  • Colon cancer treatment primarily involves surgical resection, lymphadenectomy, and adjuvant therapy (chemotherapy or radiation).
  • Curative surgery is performed for Stage I-III and Stage IV patients with resectable liver/lung metastases.
  • Surgical principles:
  • Adequate margins (≥5️ cm).
  • Complete mesocolic excision.
  • High vascular ligation.
  • Lymphadenectomy (≥1️2️ lymph nodes).
2. Segmental Resection (Colectomy)
Surgical resection is tumor-location dependent:

Key Surgical Considerations
  • Laparoscopic vs. Open Surgery: Laparoscopy preferred (same oncologic outcome, less morbidity).
  • Metastatic Disease: Explore abdomen for liver/peritoneal metastases before proceeding.
  • Lymphadenectomy: Removal of ≥1️2️ lymph nodes improves staging and survival.
  • Anastomosis Type:
  • Ileocolic (Right colectomy): Stapled preferred (lower leak rates).
  • Colocolonic & Colorectal: Surgeon’s discretion.
3. Special Considerations for Obstructing Colon Cancer
  • Patients with bowel obstruction have a worse prognosis.
  • Management Options:
  • Emergency resection with anastomosis ± diverting stoma.
  • Diverting colostomy (for high-risk patients).
  • Endoscopic stenting as a bridge to surgery (reduces emergent stomas but mixed data on long-term outcomes).
4. Adjuvant Therapy
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy is standard for Stage III colon cancer (node- positive disease).
  • Improves survival by 20-25% and reduces recurrence by 40%.
  • Regimens:
  • FOLFOX (5-Fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin).
  • CapeOx (Capecitabine, oxaliplatin).
  • Timing: Begin ~1 month after surgery (delays reduce survival).
Chemotherapy for Stage II Disease
  • Not always required but considered for high-risk Stage II:
  • Poor differentiation.
  • Lymphovascular/perineural invasion.
  • Bowel obstruction/perforation.
  • Inadequate lymphadenectomy (<12 nodes).
  • Mismatch Repair Testing:
  • Deficient MMR (dMMR/MSI-High) tumors do not benefit from 5-FU- based chemo.
Radiation Therapy
  • Rarely used for colon cancer.
  • Indications:
  • Positive/close margins after resection.
  • Locally advanced tumors with questionable clearance.

Treatment of Rectal Cancer
1. Overview
  • Stage I rectal cancer: Surgery alone is curative.
  • Stage II & III rectal cancer: High risk of local recurrence, requiring multimodal therapy:
  • Neoadjuvant chemoradiation.
  • Surgery (proctectomy).
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy.
  • Stage IV rectal cancer:
  • If resectable, multimodal therapy is used.
  • If unresectable, palliative chemotherapy ± radiation.
2. Chemotherapy & Radiation (Neoadjuvant & Adjuvant)
When to Use Chemoradiation?
  • Stage II & III rectal cancers benefit from preoperative chemoradiation.
  • Reduces local recurrence, but does not improve overall survival.
Standard Treatment Options (NCCN Guidelines)

1. Neoadjuvant chemoradiation → Surgery → Adjuvant chemotherapy.

2. Short-course radiation → Surgery → Adjuvant chemotherapy.

3. Total neoadjuvant therapy (chemotherapy + chemoradiation before

  • surgery).
Special Considerations
  • Stage IV rectal cancer:
  • If resectable, treat like stage II/III.
  • If unresectable, chemotherapy first, followed by surgery if tumor shrinks.
  • Symptomatic tumors:
  • Endoscopic fulguration or coagulation for bleeding.
  • Colostomy for impending obstruction or tenesmus.
3. Surgery for Rectal Cancer

Surgical choice depends on tumor location, size, nodal spread, and patient anatomy.

4. Local Excision
  • Indicated for small (≤3️ cm), T1N0 rectal cancers without high-risk features.
  • Techniques:
  • Transanal Excision (TAE): For low rectal tumors.
  • Transanal Endoscopic Microsurgery (TEM) & TAMIS: For higher rectal tumors.
Risks of Local Excision
  • Higher recurrence (5-year recurrence rates: 30% vs. 5% in proctectomy).
  • Risk of occult nodal metastases (~10% for T1 tumors, ~25% for T2 tumors).
  • Close follow-up required.
5. Radical Excision (Proctectomy)
Total Mesorectal Excision (TME)
  • Gold standard for rectal cancer surgery.
  • Removes entire mesorectum and lymph nodes to reduce recurrence.
  • Ensures negative circumferential margins.
1. Low Anterior Resection (LAR)
  • Used for mid-to-upper rectal tumors.
  • Restores bowel continuity (avoids colostomy).
  • Steps:
  • Resection of sigmoid colon & rectum.
  • Distal margin ≥1-2 cm.
  • Anastomosis to descending colon (straight or J-pouch).
  • Diverting ileostomy in high-risk cases (low anastomosis, poor healing).
Complications of LAR
  • Anastomotic leak (up to 15% of cases).
  • LAR syndrome (10-30%):
  • Frequent, clustered bowel movements.
  • Urgency, incontinence.
  • Worse with lower anastomoses & radiation.
  • Urinary & sexual dysfunction (nerve injury).
  • Diverting ileostomy:
  • Reduces risk of severe leaks.
  • Requires reversal surgery.
2. Abdominoperineal Resection (APR)
  • Used for low rectal tumors invading the sphincters.
  • Removes the anus, rectum, and sigmoid colon.
  • Requires permanent colostomy.
Complications of APR
  • High morbidity (up to 50%).
  • Perineal wound complications (delayed healing, infections).
  • Urinary & sexual dysfunction (due to pelvic nerve injury).
  • Perineal hernia (long-term risk, may need mesh repair).
6. Watch-and-Wait Approach
  • Used for complete clinical response after chemoradiation (no tumor visible on imaging or endoscopy).
  • Avoids surgery, but 30% risk of recurrence.
  • Requires intensive surveillance.
ProsCons
Avoids major surgery & colostomy30% recurrence rate
Better bowel & sexual functionSalvage surgery may be less effective
Lower morbidityRequires frequent follow-up

Metastatic Colorectal Cancer and Postoperative Management
1. Metastatic Disease
  • Present in ~20% of colorectal cancer patients at diagnosis.
  • Most common sites:
  • Liver (most frequent)
  • Lungs
  • Peritoneum
  • Ovaries (in women)
A. Prognosis & Treatment Goals
  • Without treatment: 5-year survival ~5%.
  • With surgical resection of metastases: 5-year survival ~30%.
  • Recurrence rate after surgery: 50-70%.
B. Systemic Chemotherapy
  • Mainstay of treatment for Stage IV colorectal cancer.
  • Standard regimens (based on 5-Fluorouracil [5-FU]):
  • FOLFOX (5-FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin)
  • FOLFIRI (5-FU, leucovorin, irinotecan)
  • CapeOX (Capecitabine, oxaliplatin)
  • Targeted therapy:
  • Bevacizumab (VEGF inhibitor) → Blocks blood vessel growth.
  • Cetuximab, Panitumumab (EGFR inhibitors) → Effective only in KRAS wild-type tumors.
C. Surgical Resection of Metastases
Indications for Surgery (Curative Intent):
  • All sites of disease can be removed completely (R0 resection).
  • Sufficient functional liver or lung tissue remains post-surgery.
  • No extrahepatic disease (except limited lung metastases).
  • Good overall performance status.
1. Liver Metastases
  • Most common metastatic site (~50% of stage IV cases).
  • Survival with resection: 30-50% at 5 years.
  • Techniques to improve resectability:
  • Portal vein embolization (PVE) – Encourages hypertrophy of the future liver remnant.
  • Staged resection – Removing tumors in phases to preserve liver function.
  • Ablative techniques (radiofrequency/microwave ablation) – Used in non-resectable cases.
2. Lung Metastases
  • Surgical resection considered if:
  • Disease is limited to the lungs.
  • No evidence of extrapulmonary spread.
  • Patient has good pulmonary reserve.
  • Alternative: Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT) (minimally invasive radiation technique).
3. Peritoneal Metastases
  • Occurs in 10-15% of cases (often from T4 or perforated tumors).
  • Poor prognosis (median survival ~22-24 months).
  • Current treatment: Systemic chemotherapy.
  • Investigational approach: Cytoreductive surgery + Hyperthermic Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy (HIPEC) → Promising but high morbidity.
2. Palliative Treatment in Unresectable Metastatic Disease
  • Goal: Improve quality of life by alleviating symptoms (obstruction, bleeding, pain).
  • Options:
  • Palliative chemotherapy (extends survival, improves symptoms).
  • Surgical bypass/diversion (for obstruction).
  • Endoscopic stenting (for obstruction in frail patients).
  • Coagulation therapy (for bleeding tumors).
  • Percutaneous drainage (for perforation).
3. Postoperative Surveillance
  • Goal: Detect recurrences early (most occur within 2-3 years post-surgery).
  • Highest risk: Within first 2 years (~60-80% of recurrences).

  • Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA):
  • If elevated postoperatively, suggests recurrence/metastasis.
  • Normal pre-op CEA may not rise even with recurrence.
  • Imaging (CT scans):

B. COLOFOL Trial Findings
  • Compared intensive vs. less-intensive surveillance.
  • No significant difference in 5-year survival.
  • Suggests that less frequent testing may be adequate in some cases.
4. Treatment for Recurrent Disease
  • Most recurrences (~50%) occur in the liver or lungs.
  • Local recurrence more common in rectal cancer.
A. Curative-Intent Surgery
  • Indicated in patients without widespread metastases.
  • R0 resection required.
  • Often combined with chemotherapy/radiation.
B. Palliative Approach
  • For unresectable recurrence, treatment includes:
  • Systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX, FOLFIRI).
  • Radiation therapy (for rectal cancer recurrences).
  • Supportive care (pain management, nutrition).
  • Prognosis with recurrence:
  • 5-year survival ~35% if resectable.
  • If unresectable, survival is limited (~12-24 months).

Neuroendocrine Tumors (NETs) of the Colon and Rectum
1. Overview
  • Neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) arise from enterochromaffin cells in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
  • Colon and rectum account for ~15% of all NETs.
  • Rectal NETs are more common than colonic NETs but have a better prognosis.
A. Symptoms & Presentation
  • Most are asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally during colonoscopy or imaging.
  • If symptomatic:
  • Rectal NETs: Rectal bleeding, changes in bowel habits.
  • Colonic NETs: Often diagnosed at an advanced stage due to vague symptoms.
B. Endoscopic Appearance
  • Submucosal nodules with normal overlying mucosa.
  • Ulcerated lesions suggest larger, more invasive tumors.
2. Prognostic Factors
  • Tumor size
  • Depth of invasion
  • Location (Rectal NETs have a better prognosis than colonic NETs).
  • Histologic subtype, grade, and mitotic index.
  • Lymphovascular invasion (high-risk feature).
A. Staging & Survival
  • Colonic NETs:
  • Often diagnosed late with 60% having metastases at presentation.
  • Worse prognosis than rectal NETs.
  • Rectal NETs:
  • Diagnosed earlier, with only 18% having metastases at presentation.
  • Better survival than colonic NETs.
3. Carcinoid Syndrome
  • Occurs in ~8% of localized colorectal NETs and ~35% of metastatic cases.
  • Due to excessive secretion of serotonin & bioactive compounds.
  • Symptoms:
  • Flushing
  • Diarrhea
  • Abdominal pain
  • Right-sided heart failure (in severe cases).
  • Why Rare in Colorectal NETs?
  • Liver metabolizes serotonin from hindgut tumors, preventing systemic symptoms.
  • Rectal NETs rarely secrete serotonin, so carcinoid syndrome is uncommon.
  • Management:
  • Octreotide (somatostatin analog) for symptomatic relief.
  • Preoperative octreotide in patients with carcinoid syndrome to prevent carcinoid crisis.
4. Diagnosis & Staging
A. Imaging Workup
  • CT Chest, Abdomen, Pelvis → Check for lymph node involvement & distant metastases.
  • Colonoscopy → Identify synchronous tumors.
  • Endorectal Ultrasound (EUS) or MRI → Staging rectal NETs.
B. Biomarkers
  • Chromogranin A (CgA)
  • 24-hour urine 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic Acid (5-HIAA) (for serotonin- producing tumors).
  • Somatostatin receptor imaging (Octreoscan/PET-CT) for metastatic disease.
5. Treatment
A. Surgical Management
Tumor TypeTreatment
Colonic NETs > 2 cmPartial colectomy + lymphadenectomy (same as
adenocarcinoma).
Colonic NETs < 2 cm, no high- risk featuresEndoscopic removal.
Rectal NETs < 1 cm (T1-T2)Endoscopic or transanal excision.
Rectal NETs > 1 cm or T3-T4 tumorsTotal mesorectal excision (TME) with lymphadenectomy.
Metastatic, resectable diseaseAttempt curative surgery.
Metastatic, unresectable diseasePalliative debulking surgery if symptomatic.
  • For unresectable metastatic disease:
  • Debulking surgery (if symptoms present).
  • Cholecystectomy recommended to prevent gallbladder disease from long-term octreotide use.
B. Adjuvant & Palliative Therapies
  • Octreotide for carcinoid syndrome.
  • Targeted therapy (everolimus, sunitinib) for metastatic NETs.
  • Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) for somatostatin receptor- positive tumors.
